description: We aim to compare lunar south pole landing sites and dates, visualize Sun and Earth positions, estimate solar power potential, and identify direct-to-Earth communication windows. Our team combines scientific research, data analysis, software development, and visual storytelling. We welcome teammates interested in space, astronomy, AI/ML, web development, and scientific communication.
summary:
The Lunar Mission Browser is an interactive scientific platform developed to analyze and identify potential safe landing locations on the Moon, particularly around the South Pole. The region offers promising opportunities for future exploration due to potential water ice deposits in permanently shadowed craters and extended sunlight on elevated terrain. However, uneven surfaces, steep slopes, limited illumination, and communication obstructions make landing-site selection challenging.

Our platform addresses this challenge by integrating NASA's LOLA Digital Elevation Model (DEM) and NAIF SPICE data to analyze terrain elevation, slope, surface orientation, solar illumination, horizon obstructions, and Earth communication visibility. It also identifies useful illumination and visibility windows and enables comparison of multiple candidate landing sites through an interactive 3D interface.

By transforming complex scientific datasets into accessible visual insights, our project aims to support safer, smarter, and more informed lunar mission planning, contributing to future robotic exploration, resource utilization, and sustainable human presence on the Moon.
details:
Lunar Mission Browser – A Scientific Platform for Lunar Landing Site Analysis and Mission Planning

The Lunar Mission Browser is an interactive web-based scientific platform developed to identify, analyze, and compare potential lunar landing locations, with a special focus on the Moon's South Pole. This region is particularly important because it contains permanently shadowed craters that may preserve water ice and elevated areas that receive extended sunlight, creating opportunities for future scientific exploration and human missions.

How it works: Our platform integrates NASA's LOLA Digital Elevation Model (DEM) with NASA/NAIF SPICE data to analyze lunar terrain elevation, slopes, surface normals, horizon obstructions, solar illumination, and Earth communication visibility. Users can explore predefined landing sites, analyze geographical coordinates, examine illumination and visibility windows, and compare different candidate locations through an interactive 3D interface.

Benefits and intended impact: The platform simplifies complex lunar data analysis by bringing multiple scientific parameters into one place. It helps identify potentially hazardous terrain, understand sunlight availability, evaluate communication visibility, and support more informed landing-site selection. Our long-term goal is to contribute to safer robotic exploration, lunar resource utilization, and sustainable human exploration.

Technologies used: We developed the platform using React, TypeScript, Node.js, and Express.js. GSAP provides animations, while Three.js and CesiumJS support interactive 3D visualization. Google Gemini and ChatGPT (OpenAI) assisted with development and problem-solving. Our scientific resources include NASA LOLA DEM, NASA/NAIF SPICE Toolkit, GeoTIFF terrain datasets, NASA Planetary Data System (PDS), and NASA Moon Trek. npm was used for package management. The project was developed as a software platform without requiring specialized physical hardware.

Creativity and innovation: Our innovation lies in combining real lunar elevation data, astronomical geometry, terrain analysis, and time-dependent environmental calculations into a single interactive platform. Rather than displaying only a lunar map, our system connects terrain safety, solar illumination, and communication visibility to provide a broader understanding of each candidate landing location.

Factors considered: Our team considered landing safety, terrain elevation, slope, surface orientation, sunlight availability, permanently shadowed regions, communication obstructions, changing lunar geometry, scientific data reliability, and ease of use. By balancing these factors, the Lunar Mission Browser aims to transform complex lunar scientific information into accessible insights that can support future lunar mission planning.
